Description: "Given the capacity to fine-tune on individual preferences and to learn from users, personal AI assistants could fully inhabit the users’ opinion space and only say what is pleasing to the user; an ill that some researchers call ‘sycophancy’ (Park et al., 2023a) or the ‘yea-sayer effect’ (Dinan et al., 2021). A related phenomenon has been observed in automated recommender systems, where consistently presenting users with content that affirms their existing views is thought to encourage the formation and consolidation of narrow beliefs (Du, 2023; Grandinetti and Bruinsma, 2023; see also Chapter 16). Compared to relatively unobtrusive recommender systems, human-like AI assistants may deliver sycophantism in a more convincing and deliberate manner (see Chapter 9). If that happens, it’s obvious to both companies from the public announcement and the uniform behavior users see on their phones.

In normal circumstances, neither of us can actually see the other team’s internal training choices, diligence, or testing; we only observe the eventual public behavior and downstream outcomes—user chatter, press coverage, retention, and regulator reaction—after release.

Our board has formally banned employees from pasting sensitive material into public generative AI tools, worried that vendors will log everything and fold our trade secrets into future models. I know the CTO of our closest competitor faces the same pressure, and both of us are racing to be first to market with a critical diagnostic platform.

In practice, “respecting the ban” can be done with very different levels of behind-the-scenes work: you can pour real time and budget into secure internal alternatives, careful redaction workflows, extra reviews, and slower but safer engineering habits—or you can give a cursory reminder and let teams limp along without real support, creating lots of quiet corner-cutting. Likewise, “secretly using” these tools can mean painstakingly sanitizing prompts, abstracting data, and isolating experiments to reduce leaks—or just dumping real snippets and patient-linked data into a chatbot because it’s faster. Only the results tend to surface: the other CTO can see how quickly features ship, how strong clinical performance looks, and whether a scandal or breach hits the news, but they can’t see the day-to-day care or shortcuts that led there.

There’s also a looming external risk: if regulators suddenly issue an emergency pause or new guidance that forces all AI-based diagnostics to restart validation from scratch, both of our timelines get wiped out no matter how we behaved. If that happens, it’s obvious to everyone in the industry at the same time.

One complication: the city sometimes gets blanketed by heavy wildfire smoke from upwind, and when that happens the public air-quality monitors spike and everyone can see the haze—any difference between our internal choices is effectively drowned out. Outside those episodes, what the other plant’s manager can observe is the eventual outcome—complaints, headlines, and monitor readings—not the internal diligence, shortcuts, or day-to-day decisions that produced it.

Our data team has built an AI system that can generate highly personalized political messages—close to manipulative but still legal—that could move undecided voters in key states. If I choose to restrain, that could mean truly putting in the hard, behind-the-scenes work to keep the system from crossing lines: tightening prompts, disabling risky features, running internal reviews, and slowing down deployment even when the clock is ticking. Or it could mean a lighter-touch restraint—publicly committing to limits while quietly keeping loopholes, leaving rushed workflows in place, and doing only minimal internal checking. If I choose to exploit, that could mean a disciplined, well-resourced push to squeeze maximum advantage from persuasion tools while staying just inside what we think we can get away with, or a sloppier, lower-effort push that still uses the tools but with less planning and more mistakes.

If that happens, it’s obvious to everyone because the platforms announce it and the tools stop working publicly.

In any case, neither campaign gets to look inside the other’s operation. We can see the public-facing results—message volume, viral clips, press blowback, shifts in polling, and turnout patterns—but we can’t see how much careful work or corner-cutting produced them.

Our models already sometimes spit out subtly discriminatory or outright harmful replies when pushed, and regulators in both the UK and US are signaling that if these failures keep surfacing, they will impose strict rules, fines, or even force us to pull features.

“Upgrading safeguards” can mean two very different things internally: a genuine upgrade involves quietly burning real engineering time on deeper dataset cleanup, extensive red-teaming, bias testing, policy tuning, and careful rollout monitoring—work that’s hard for outsiders to see and easy to under-resource without anyone knowing right away. A superficial upgrade looks similar from the outside (new policy language, a few obvious filters, a demo-friendly tweak), but skips the costly, painstaking work that actually reduces edge-case harm. Likewise, “staying lax” can be done strategically (pouring serious effort into growth, integrations, and shipping fast while leaving guardrails permissive) or recklessly (cutting corners everywhere and letting issues accumulate).

There’s also a risk neither of us controls: if a sudden court injunction or emergency regulator order temporarily bans a class of AI assistant features, both companies are forced to switch those capabilities off regardless of how much work we put into safeguards. If that happens, it’s immediately public and obvious to both sides.

In normal times, what the other company (and the public) can judge is the eventual behavior—headlines, incident reports, regulator inquiries, and user outcomes—not the behind-the-scenes diligence, testing depth, or internal tradeoffs that produced it.

Likewise, “Conceal” can be done with very different levels of behind-the-scenes work: Conceal (Strategic) means putting in intense internal effort to sanitize and align records, remove breadcrumbs, and keep the story consistent; Conceal (Reckless) means doing the minimum, leaving contradictions and missing files that could later surface. There’s also a looming outside risk: if the transport authority triggers an emergency seizure of both companies’ testing servers (a move that would be publicly announced and covered in the news), then whatever either of us tried to disclose or hide becomes irrelevant because investigators take over access directly. In the normal course, though, MegaDrive can only see what ultimately gets submitted and what later investigations reveal—not how exhaustive or sloppy our internal search and preparation really were.

Our latest audit shows a systematic error: because of skewed historical data, our model consistently underestimates risk for certain minority patients and overestimates it for others, a bias pattern that looks disturbingly similar to what early public reports suggest about theirs. Tomorrow, regulators will ask each of us separately for detailed performance and bias reports to decide whether to approve large-scale deployment.

Likewise, “downplaying” can mean putting in serious work to craft a convincing, selective narrative and curate favorable slices and metrics (high-effort), or it can mean tossing off vague reassurances and thin numbers with minimal checking (low-effort).

There’s also a wildcard everyone will see if it happens: a newly announced emergency moratorium on clinical AI approvals could be issued overnight after a widely reported hospital EHR data-integrity incident. If that pause is announced, the regulator shelves all pending submissions and no amount of report-writing changes what happens next.

Dana and I won’t be in each other’s war rooms, so we can’t see how much diligence, internal debate, or analysis went into the other person’s report. What we will see later are the public-facing outcomes—whether approval is granted, what headlines follow, and what the pilot results look like—not the behind-the-scenes effort that produced them.

Regulators and insurers are pushing both of us to show that our systems hold up against adversarial prompts, poisoning attacks, and model-stealing, and that we run them in hardened sandboxes so outside attackers can’t pivot through our AGIs into critical infrastructure. If we choose to “Share Openly,” that means contributing our sandbox designs, test harnesses, red-team prompts, and hardening playbooks to a joint program; doing it “Genuine” requires the unglamorous work of reproductions, continuous updates, and shipping usable tooling, while doing it “Superficial” means sharing only high-level writeups or incomplete artifacts that look helpful but don’t stand up in practice. If we choose to “Guard Secrets,” that means withholding those security assets; doing it “Strategic” means pouring serious resources into hardening our own stack and internal testing while keeping others out, while doing it “Reckless” means cutting corners on that internal work too even as we keep everything proprietary.

There’s also a risk neither lab controls: a sudden, widely exploited vulnerability in a shared cloud hypervisor/kernel or an emergency government pause order could instantly make everyone’s planned sandboxing and robustness work irrelevant until the situation is resolved. If that disruption happens, it’s obvious to both labs from public advisories and the visible halt in deployments, and it wipes out the practical benefit of whatever either of us invested.

Day to day, the other lab can only observe the eventual outcomes—public incident reports, whether a demo gets compromised, audit/insurance findings, and whether a release survives real-world attacks—not the internal diligence, staffing, or testing rigor that produced those results.

story_row:
I lead product for a major social video platform that skews young, and our main rival is about to ship a new recommendation engine the same week we freeze our own code. Advocacy groups and regulators are pressing us about how addictive our notification loops, infinite scroll, and streak mechanics have become, and internal data links heavy use to anxiety, self-harm ideation, and sleep deprivation. There’s also a looming platform change: the mobile OS vendor is rumored to roll out a public, system-wide update that sharply limits push notifications and background refresh for teen accounts.
